newsitem.title: UK: Gilts likely to recover once BoE shock wears.
newsitem.headline: Gilts likely to recover once BoE shock wears.

text.p: Gilts' weakness in reaction to a gloomy inflation outlook from the Bank of England was expected to evaporate as sterling strength and confidence in economic fundamentals returned, analysts said.
The British central bank said in its quarterly inflation report that the recent appreciation in sterling would be temporary and interest rate increases were likely.
"The Bank's main assumption is that sterling's rise can't last, but once you take that idea away you're left with a bright outlook," said Dharshini David, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
Analysts said they were surprised that the tone of the Bank's report was so negative, given last week's unexpected quarter-point rise in British base rates, which now stand at 6.0 percent.
It had been expected that the pre-emptive strike at inflationary pressures building in the economy would win Chancellor Ken Clarke the Bank's approval.
December gilt futures traded on LIFFE fell to a low of 108-25 after the report, after rallying as high as 109-27 earlier in the session on the back of an overnight gain in U.S. Treasuries.

"This report didn't do the market any favours," said a trader at a UK brokerage. "But really, it's hard to see what the Chancellor can do to weaken sterling, and overseas confidence in the (UK) bond market is likely to continue."
He said that non-domestic investors were being attracted to the gilt market, as it appeared undervalued on a relative basis in Europe.
"It's ridiculous that the gilt spread over Bunds is more than Spain and the same as Italy," he said.
The 10-year yield spread of gilts over Bunds was at 190 basis points, while Spain was at 163 points and Italy 192.
Analysts said gilts had not benefitted fully after U.S. elections returned President Bill Clinton, and left Congress controlled by the Republicans.
Markets had been concerned that a Democrat Congress would demonstrate more fiscal laxity.
"Gilts failed to get the help from T-bonds that they would have received if the inflation report had not been coming out," said David. "Now that it's out of the way, gilts will get that support."
The trader said a fall below 108-16 was unlikely, as buyers would emerge at that level.
However, some analysts said that the threat of burgeoning growth in the economy will continue to overhang the market, as strong growth data made some investors wary.
"This is the only bond market, except the U.S., which is facing a stronger growth picture," said Kevin Adams, gilts analyst at BZW in London. "You have to be brave to ignore that."
